summary: Give the Exoplanet discovery calculator the orbital period and the redshift and it returns area (Information about the star). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Exoplanet discovery calculator work?
sections.html:
The Exoplanet discovery calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports area (Information about the star) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the detection method, select a star and select a planet); then you type in the orbital period and the redshift.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

  • A measured quantity, entered by default in days. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Show area”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • A single on/off switch — tick it for “Show orbital speed / period”, leave it clear for the other case. It changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 7 options, such as red, orange and yellow. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.
  • Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as yes please! and no thanks. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.

7 fields on this form are a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Exoplanet discovery calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Area=PI × (radius ^ 2)
Area=100 × area ÷ star appear dimmer by up to
Orbital speed of the star=299792458 × redshift
M sum=orbital radius × (mass) ÷ (orbital radius − wiggle)
Insqrt=(1 ÷ 4) × (orbital period ^ 2) ÷ (PI ^ 2)
Orbital speed of the star=2 × PI × wiggle ÷ (orbital period)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Length, opening in Sun radii
  • Mass, opening in masses of the Sun
  • Area, opening in square kilometers
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Length, opening in Earth radii
  • Mass, opening in masses of the Earth
  • Length, opening in astronomical units
  • Time, opening in days

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Exoplanet discovery calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the orbital period and the redshift — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Exoplanet discovery calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns area (Information about the star), derived from the orbital period and the redshift. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Exoplanet discovery calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the orbital period and the redshift, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter radius (Information about the star) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Radius (Information about the star) opens in Sun radii and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (7 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Radius = 0 R☉. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Exoplanet discovery calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
